author: james-nesbitt
body:
Fixes #417.

## What

Pass `--allow-vendor-change` on the zypper **install** action in `NewZypper`, so `PackageManager.Install` succeeds non-interactively when the only dependency-resolution solution replaces a package from a different vendor.

## Why

rig always runs zypper's non-interactive install (`zypper install -y`). By default zypper will not switch a package's vendor during an install, and non-interactively it does not accept the vendor-changing solution — it cancels and exits 4, with no actionable error. This affects any rig consumer installing a package whose resolution crosses a vendor boundary on SLES/openSUSE; it is not specific to any tool, repo, or package. Full mechanism, repro, and logs are in #417.

## ⚠️ This may be undesirable — RFC

**This change is deliberately aggressive about package adoption.** Passing `--allow-vendor-change` unconditionally lets zypper switch a package's vendor/origin on any install, which some operators may consider undesirable as a global default (it weakens the same-vendor guarantee zypper gives out of the box).

Raising as an RFC. If a global default isn't acceptable, the alternative is to gate it behind an opt-in install option — but that requires extending `PackageManager.Install` (today `Install(ctx, packageNames ...string)`, no room for per-call options), a larger, breaking-ish API change affecting every manager and caller. Happy to implement whichever shape you prefer; this one-line version is the minimal demonstration.

## Testing

- `go build ./packagemanager/...` and `go test ./packagemanager/...` pass.
- Manually verified on a SLES 15 instance: the un-flagged install exits 4 on a vendor-change resolution, and the same install with `--allow-vendor-change` succeeds (exit 0).

body:
Audit des deux tests visés par l'avis 3 étoiles (compatibilité amoureuse et points communs) sur le scoring, les traductions et les conclusions, dans les 5 langues.

## Ce qui était déjà bon

Le calcul du score est juste, et je n'ai rien inventé pour meubler :

- le pourcentage vaut le nombre de réponses identiques sur 20, deux joueurs qui répondent pareil obtiennent bien **100 %**, deux joueurs qui divergent partout obtiennent **0 %** (vérifié en direct dans les 5 langues) ;
- les paliers couvrent la plage complète sans trou ni chevauchement ;
- les 20 questions de compatibilité et les 30 premières questions de points communs sont **traduites nativement dans les 5 langues**, options alignées une à une, aucune fuite de français ;
- les seuls libellés identiques au français en anglais, espagnol, allemand et italien sont des mots qui s'écrivent pareil (Pizza, Sushi, Thriller, New York) ;
- aucune erreur JS sur ces deux tests, dans aucune des 5 langues.

## Les trois problèmes réels

### 1. Le test de compatibilité affichait les verdicts d'un autre quiz

Il utilisait les verdicts génériques du quiz de goûts, « Vos goûts se ressemblent énormément », alors qu'il interroge le mariage, les enfants, l'argent, la fidélité, la carrière et le lieu de vie. Ces verdicts découpaient en plus le score en tiers (0-30 / 35-65 / 70-100 %), en contradiction directe avec la grille de lecture affichée sur la page elle-même (80-100 / 60-80 / 40-60 / moins de 40). Le palier « âmes sœurs » annoncé n'était donc **jamais atteignable**, et un couple à 75 % lisait « Sur la même longueur d'onde » quand la page lui promettait « Belle compatibilité ».

Le test reçoit ses quatre verdicts dédiés, écrits pour un test de valeurs et traduits dans les 5 langues, bornés exactement sur la grille publiée :

| Score | Verdict |
|---|---|
| 80 % et plus | Âmes sœurs |
| 60 à 79 % | Une belle compatibilité |
| 40 à 59 % | Une compatibilité à cultiver |
| Moins de 40 % | Des chemins différents |

La grille de la page est reformulée en même temps pour supprimer le chevauchement des bornes (« 60-80 » et « 40-60 » se recouvraient).

Chaque verdict rappelle explicitement que le pourcentage mesure des réponses alignées et non la force du couple, dans la continuité du correctif de l'avis une étoile espagnol.

### 2. Un palier visuel désaccordé du verdict

L'emoji et le fond du résultat suivaient un seuil de pourcentage parallèle à celui des verdicts. À **7/20 exactement (35 %)**, le titre positif « Beaucoup de points communs » s'affichait sous l'emoji dubitatif 🤔 et le fond du palier bas. L'emoji, le fond et les confettis découlent désormais du verdict retenu, donc plus aucun écart possible.

### 3. Le test de points communs promettait 200 questions et en servait 30

La promesse était partout : title, meta description, badge du hero, un H2 entier, la FAQ et les données structurées `totalQuestions`, dans les 5 langues. La réalité : les questions 31 à 200 existaient bien en anglais, espagnol, allemand et italien, mais sans aucun lien vers leurs options, et n'existaient pas du tout en français. Le moteur les écartait donc en silence.

Conséquence concrète pour l'utilisateur : 20 questions tirées dans un pool de 30, donc **13 questions sur 20 déjà vues** en rejouant une deuxième fois, alors que la page promet « une expérience unique à chaque fois ».

Correctif :

- support des options mutualisées dans le chargeur (la question porte la liste des identifiants, chaque libellé vit une seule fois) ;
- les 170 questions manquantes et les 59 libellés d'options écrits en français ;
- mappage des options des questions 31 à 200 dans les 5 langues ;
- dix questions qui faisaient doublon avec les trente premières (cuisiner, sport, séries, lire, jeux de société, randonnée, musique live, introverti/extraverti, ponctualité, coucher tôt) remplacées par dix questions inédites dans les 5 langues, pour garder 200 questions réellement distinctes ;
- pool porté de 30 à 200.

Recouvrement mesuré entre deux parties après correctif : **1 à 5 questions sur 20** au lieu de 13. La distribution du score est inchangée (environ 33 % de réponses identiques attendues au hasard avant comme après), donc les paliers restent calibrés.

## Au passage

Suppression des tirets cadratins restants dans le contenu visible : compatibilité, distance, Z'Amours, accueil et quiz personnalisé, dans les 5 langues.

## Vérifications

- 200 questions jouables, alignées et sans fuite de français dans les 5 langues (audit sur les fichiers construits, pas sur les sources).
- Parties jouées en direct sur les deux tests dans les 5 langues, aux bornes 0, 35, 40, 60, 80 et 100 %, verdict et palier visuel contrôlés à chaque fois.
- Balayage de régression complet : **30 quiz en français, 30/30 résultats atteints, 0 erreur JS** et **100 exécutions en anglais, espagnol, allemand et italien, 100/100 vertes, 0 erreur JS, 0 marqueur français détecté**.
- Build : 333 pages, 0 échec.

Task 5.3 of the CrewAI × Gmail Ingestion PoC. `--demo` runs the full ingestion pipeline (fetch → parse → summarize → `SummaryRecord`) end-to-end against committed fixtures — no Gmail credentials, no LLM API key, byte-identical output across repeat runs. Target: `main`.

## Design — Option B (end-to-end with monkey-patched LLM)

Chose the literal AC interpretation over the "skip CrewAI" shortcut. Rationale: `--demo` doubles as a smoke test proving CrewAI orchestration works with a deterministic LLM; skipping it would forfeit that coverage.

- **LLM**: `NativeAnthropicLLM.call` is monkey-patched at demo-batch scope to return canned `Summary` JSONs from `tests/fixtures/emails/llm_responses.json`, keyed by the currently-processing `message_id`. A module-level context variable (`_DEMO_CURRENT_MESSAGE_ID`) is set before each `flow.kickoff` and cleared in a `finally` — never leaks across iterations.
- **Gmail**: bypassed via a tiny duck-typed `_DemoGmailReader` that answers `get_message` from an in-memory dict of the fixture payloads.
- **Telemetry opt-out**: `CREWAI_TELEMETRY_OPT_OUT=1` set at module import — mirrors the ordering invariant in `main._bootstrap`.
- **Determinism**: `SummaryRecord.created_at` is frozen to `DEMO_CREATED_AT` via `model_copy` after each kickoff. Monkey-patching `_utcnow` would be a no-op — Pydantic captures the `default_factory` at class-definition time — so we rebuild the instance.
- **Tokens**: stay at `(None, None)`. The mocked `call()` bypasses `_record_usage` entirely. Documented + tested.

## AC ↔ Implementation

| Task 5.3 AC | Delivered |
|---|---|
| `--demo` bypasses Gmail (no token.json) | `_DemoGmailReader` in-memory reader |
| Fixture loader reads `tests/fixtures/emails/*.json` as `RawMessage` | `iter_demo_messages` |
| LLM monkey-patched at demo bootstrap, keyed by `message_id` | `_demo_llm_call` + `_DEMO_CURRENT_MESSAGE_ID` context |
| Pipeline runs end-to-end producing `SummaryRecord` | Full `MailIngestorFlow` executed |
| Output → `demo/00N_sample.json` (not stdout) | `run_demo_batch(fixtures_dir, output_dir)` |
| Two back-to-back runs produce byte-identical output | `model_copy(update={"created_at": DEMO_CREATED_AT})` + sorted fixture iteration |
| `llm_responses.json` ≤ 20 KB | Actual size: 3,058 bytes |

## Files

**New:**
- `src/mail_ingestor/demo.py` (~150 LOC) — loader, LLM adapter, orchestrator
- `tests/fixtures/emails/00{1..5}_*.json` — 5 Gmail resource dicts (weekly report, meeting recap, invoice, newsletter, reminder)
- `tests/fixtures/emails/llm_responses.json` — 5 canned Summary payloads (3 KB)
- `tests/fixtures/emails/poison_missing_headers.json` — reserved for Story 5.4's cross-cutting DLQ test; skipped by `iter_email_paths` via the `poison_` prefix
- `demo/00{1..5}_sample.json` — the deterministic committed output a fresh contributor sees after running `python -m mail_ingestor.main --demo`
- `tests/test_demo.py` — 21 tests

**Modified:**
- `src/mail_ingestor/main.py` — `--demo` branch dispatches to `run_demo_batch` (was stub error). No `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` required.
- `tests/test_cli_main.py` — old stub test replaced with dispatch + no-auth-required assertions.

## Test coverage — 21 new (283 total)

- **Fixture loader** (6): 5 emails yielded, poison + llm_responses skipped, sort-order determinism, missing-id fixture rejected, RawMessage roundtrip
- **LLM responses loader** (4): keyed by message_id, Summary-shaped entries, top-level-list rejection, **20 KB ceiling guard**, every fixture has a matching response
- **LLM adapter** (3): no-context RuntimeError, canned lookup, unknown-id `DemoLookupError`
- **End-to-end `run_demo_batch`** (8): file-per-fixture, SummaryRecord validation, `created_at` frozen, tokens stay None, **byte-identical determinism**, context cleared after loop, output_dir auto-created, no-`ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` needed
- **CLI dispatch** (2): `--demo` returns 0, no auth token required

## Live smoke

```
$ rm -rf demo/ && uv run python -m mail_ingestor.main --demo
2026-08-04 12:12:10 INFO mail_ingestor.demo demo_written ... message_id=demo-msg-001
... (5 lines) ...
2026-08-04 12:12:10 INFO mail_ingestor.demo demo_batch_complete count=5

$ md5 demo/*.json | sort > /tmp/h1
$ rm -rf demo/ && uv run python -m mail_ingestor.main --demo >/dev/null 2>&1
$ md5 demo/*.json | sort | diff - /tmp/h1
$ # empty diff → byte-identical
```

## Validation

- pytest: **283 pass** (259 → +24)
- mypy --strict on all 10 core files: **clean** (one narrow `arg-type` ignore on `_DemoGmailReader` — duck-typing; `GmailReaderService` should become a `Protocol` in a later cleanup)
- ruff: **clean**
- CrewAI fence: **2 files** (`flow.py` + `tools/gmail_tool.py`), unchanged

author: jhso-dev
body:
A company that already runs OpenSearch for logs and search can point yoke at it: `YOKE_OPENSEARCH_URL`, and every screen, every MCP tool and every CLI command works on top of it.

The value beyond the feature is what it cost. **No change to the port, the composite, or `openStore`'s structure.** `RemoteStore` was declared as a *shape* rather than a base class in v5.2, on the theory that a second remote adapter would satisfy it without importing the composite. That was a claim in a comment; it is now tested.

## No dependency

OpenSearch is REST, so this takes a `fetchImpl` the way the qdrant adapter does. neo4j needed `neo4j-driver-lite` (3.8 MB) because Bolt is a binary protocol — here the seam that makes the adapter fakeable is the same one that makes it free.

## Four policies, each measured against a real 2.19 server *before* it was written

**Reads refresh before they read.** OpenSearch is near-real-time: a write is durable immediately and *searchable* only after a refresh (~1s). The port contract is read-your-writes, and `?refresh=true` per write forces a segment flush per document — the bounded-search conformance case alone writes 1,005 of them. So writes mark their index dirty and the next READ refreshes once. That case runs in **2.3s**.

**Prefix terms are required, exact terms are what score.** A Lucene `prefix` query is constant-score, so a query built only from prefixes satisfies "matches" and silently fails "best match first" — the exact trap the neo4j adapter hit with wildcards. And prefix matching is not optional here:

```
match  '재시도'   → 0건     (against text containing '재시도는')
match  '재시도는'  → 1건
```

The standard analyzer keeps the particle attached, and OpenSearch ships no Korean morphological analyzer by default (`nori` is a separate plugin). A test pins the stem lookup.

**Vectors live in their own index, keyed by entity id.** Measured first: with vectors on the entity documents, a k-NN search returned the same record *once per version*. Keying by id makes `putEmbedding` a derived-index write that creates no version and invalidates no citation — the same reason sqlite has `entity_vec` and neo4j has `(:EntityVec)`. There is a test for the duplicate.

**`latest` is a stored flag, not a query-time collapse.** `collapse` + `search_after` can approximate latest-version-only enumeration, but a `status` filter would then match *any* version rather than the one being returned.

## The suite can run against a cluster that is holding a demo

Scoped by index prefix — it creates and deletes `yoketest_*` only. Verified by running all 30 cases against the same cluster while a **1,007-document corpus sat in `yoke_*`**, and counting it unchanged afterwards.

Neo4j Community has one database per server, so its suite has to erase everything. That warning stays in `docs/BACKENDS.md`; this contrast is now written next to it.

## Both remote variables at once is an error

Not a precedence order. Two databases, two corpora — picking one silently means `yoke inject` answering out of a store the caller did not think they were using.

## Demo, loaded and screenshotted

504 records committed through the real gate into OpenSearch (260 base + 108 aged-out + 108 in 54 contradicting pairs), 30 people, 10 collaborations, 1,272 relations, 517 vectors at 1024 dimensions:

- **stale queue**: 132 aged out, routed across **30 distinct owners**
- **conflicts**: 68 unresolved pairs
- **graph**: renders, truncation banner honest at the 200-node cap
- **hybrid retrieval**: keyword-only 0 hits on all three Korean questions, hybrid answers each at rank 1–2

## Also in here

**qdrant verified against a real server for the first time** — 21/21 on the shared conformance cases. It had only ever passed against its in-memory REST fake, which is defensible for a JSON filter surface and is still not the same claim. And the Postgres read-mapping against a real PG 16.14: mapped, FK-linked, idempotent on re-sync.

## Checks

typecheck · lint · `test:main` 466 · **opensearch 30/30 (live)** · neo4j 28/28 (live, on a second instance so the demo survived) · kuzu 22/22 · `test:bundle` · `eval` unchanged. New CI job `opensearch-adapter` with a service container and a non-vacuity step, matching the neo4j job.

author: timohueser
body:
**B1 of #1116.** C4's re-measurement left the browser's peak as three terms, of which the engine is now only ~45 %: the input cells and the output set, each fully resident in wasm memory, are the ceiling. This halves the output term — from the whole set resident until `takeFile`, to **at most one shard**.

## The seam

In `obcm-assemble`'s write/verify loop, `store.source(i)` is called *only* inside the iteration that wrote shard `i`. After that §4.8 pass returns, `check_set_invariants` and the manifest are built from `plans` — nothing reads those bytes again. So the next `begin(i+1)`, or the `manifest` call, is an observable "shard `i` is dead weight" signal that a `ShardStore` can act on without the engine knowing. **The engine is unchanged** (the one thing this PR uses from it, `shard::shard_filename`, was already `pub`).

```rust
trait Hooks {
    fn wants_shards(&self) -> bool { false }
    fn take_shard(&mut self, shard: OutputFile) -> Result<Option<OutputFile>, String> { Ok(Some(shard)) }
}
```

### Why opt-in, and why in two halves

A default that silently drops bytes is a footgun, so the default hands the shard straight back: `NoHooks`, the native determinism suite and every existing caller keep the whole set in `Outcome::files`, byte for byte. `Ok(None)` means taken; `Err(msg)` means the sink failed and the bytes are already gone, which fails the run as `io` rather than finish a set with a hole in it and call it a map.

`wants_shards` is separate from `take_shard` for one reason: it also gates the hashing (below), and a caller that keeps everything should pay exactly what it paid before. The pairing is a footgun of its own — an override of `take_shard` alone would silently do nothing — so it is pinned by a test (`a_caller_that_does_not_ask_is_handed_nothing`) rather than left to the doc comment.

### Hash at write

A hand-off happens *mid-run*, before `Summary` exists, so the store derives the §5.2 filename itself and hashes the bytes as they are written (`sha2`, the same crate and version the engine already hashes shards with — no new bundle weight), finalizing at `seal`. Both are compared against `summary.shards[i]` when the run ends; a disagreement is `internal`. That is a tripwire, not a gate — by then the shard is gone — but the mid-run name and digest are what a caller writes onto a card, so being right about them is a correctness claim. It also means the comparison is a real check rather than a restatement: the digest is of the buffer the store actually accumulated, arrived at by a different path than the engine's.

Aborts are unchanged, and a cancelled run may already have handed shards out — the caller's cleanup. Safe by construction rather than by cleanup: the OBCS manifest is written **last** (§5.4), so a partial set is not a map to a device however many `.OBM` files it has. The terrain shard (written through the engine's own sink, not the store) and the manifest keep their end-of-run path.

## What the browser's peak looks like now

engine + input cells + **one 256 MB shard**, instead of engine + input + the whole set. `forceSplit: true` and `targetShardBytes: 256 MB` come from the builder's run request; 256 MB is the largest piece the download screen is willing to have resident and a plausible resumable-upload/card-write unit, against the engine's 1 GiB default (§5's 32-shard ceiling is the other end of that range).

`estimate.rs` is deliberately **not** touched (it is #1123's, and it is still in flight): the projection keeps pricing the old shape, which is the conservative direction for a threshold whose job is to refuse. Loosening it wants a measurement, not an argument.

## Worker protocol

A new `shard` message — same fields as `file`, buffer in the transfer list — with two differences that matter to B2:

* **No ack.** The callback runs inside the synchronous wasm call; the worker cannot await anything from in there. `file` keeps its `file-ack` backpressure; `shard` posts and the run carries on.
* **It arrives before `planned`.** The set plan does not exist until the run ends.

Which is why the **device path does not opt in**: `sendAssembledSetFile` opens its transfer from `planned`'s shard count and byte total, so streaming to a device is real protocol work rather than a flag. It keeps today's behaviour exactly (whole set resident, acked files) and is a B-series follow-up.

## The sink, per host

Files now arrive during the run, so the screen's saves are serialized through a promise chain (unacked messages can overlap, and `openMapOutput` is a lazily-opened folder that must not be opened twice).

* **Desktop** — each part is written into the one output folder as it lands; `discard()` on cancel or failure removes the folder. `failRun` waits for the one possibly-in-flight write first, so the discard cannot race a file being written into the directory it is removing.
* **Web** — each file is staged as a Blob (browsers may spill those to disk) and handed to the downloader only once the set is complete. Saving each shard as it landed would drop half a map into someone's Downloads folder the moment they pressed cancel. **OPFS staging is B2's job**; this is deliberately the cheap version, and the wasm-side memory — the thing the budget is about — is freed either way.
* **Both** — "discard the N files you downloaded" now counts what actually reached the disk, not what the assembler handed over. A cancelled browser run says "nothing was saved", because nothing was.

## Verification

* `cargo test -p obc-web-assemble --release` — 23 tests. The determinism suite now covers eviction: `the_evicted_stream_plus_the_remainder_is_the_native_clis_volume_set` asserts the streamed shards (in delivery order) followed by the end-of-run remainder are the committed CLI fixture set, name by name and byte by byte, and that only terrain + manifest are left in the store. Plus the single-file path, the hand-back path, the never-asked path, a refusing sink (`io`, sink's own message, first shard already gone), and a cancel that has already handed one over.
* `bridge.test.ts` — the same pin against the **wasm** build from Node, including that the three shards are gone from `fileCount` while the summary still lists them, that each streamed digest is the manifest's, and that a throwing sink fails as `io`.
* `cargo test --release` + `cargo build --release` workspace green; `cargo fmt --all`; clippy clean on the crate for both host and `wasm32-unknown-unknown`.
* CI's `web` job locally: `npm run check` (0 errors), `npm test` (789 tests), `npm run build:all`. `wasm_size_guard.py --module assemble`: 208 KB gzipped / 225 KB budget, 486 KB raw / 524 KB budget — ok.
* No end-to-end smoke: an actual browser assembly needs a live catalog to download cells from, which a worktree does not have. The wasm path is covered by `bridge.test.ts` against the real module instead.

## Docs

`formats.md` said a browser run "has to hold the cells, the finished set and the graph rewrite's working memory at once" — now stale for the download path. Fixed in a separate `docs:` commit as an added paragraph next to the projection (not a rewrite of it) so it does not fight #1123 over the same sentences, plus one clause in the crate's own line in the further-reading list. `--check-links` clean.

body:
## Problem

The `msteamsV2` task supports only `createConversation` and `replyToConversation` — there is no way to update a posted activity in place. The Bot Framework supports this via `PUT {rootApi}/{conversationId}/activities/{activityId}`, the same base URL `replyToConversation` already builds plus one path segment and a different HTTP verb.

## Use case

Live-updating status cards: a flow posts an Adaptive Card (e.g. PR checks/approvals status) and later rebuilds and replaces it in place, instead of accumulating thread replies for every state change.

## What changed

- **`TeamsV2TaskParams.java`** — new `UPDATEACTIVITY` action, new `UpdateActivityParams` (extends `ReplayToConversationParams`, adds required `activityId`), and the corresponding `of()` dispatch case.
- **`TeamsClientV2.java`** — `exec(Map, String)` refactored into `exec(Map, String, String method)` using `HttpRequest.Builder.method(...)`; the old two-arg signature delegates to `"POST"`, so existing behavior is unchanged. New `updateActivity(activity, rootApi, conversationId, activityId)` builds `{rootApi}/{conversationId}/activities/{activityId}` and issues a `PUT`.
- **`TeamsV2TaskCommon.java`** — `UPDATEACTIVITY` switch case and an `updateActivity(...)` handler with the same error/`ignoreErrors` semantics as `replyToConversation`.
- **`CommonV2Test.java`** — new tests assert the request verb is `PUT`, the URL is `{rootApi}/{conversationId}/activities/{activityId}`, a success response maps to `result.ok == true`, and a missing `activityId` throws. All existing tests pass unmodified.

Note on status codes: `exec` previously accepted only `201` as success. The Bot Framework's update-activity endpoint returns `200 OK`, so the new `PUT` path also accepts `200` (`Constants.TEAMS_SUCCESS_STATUS_CODE`). POST paths keep the exact 201-only check.

## Example flow

```yaml
flows:
  updateStatusCard:
    - task: msteamsV2
      in:
        action: updateActivity
        conversationId: ${createResult.conversationId}
        activityId: ${createResult.activityId}
        activity:
          type: message
          attachments:
            - contentType: application/vnd.microsoft.card.adaptive
              content:
                type: AdaptiveCard
                version: "1.4"
                body:
                  - type: TextBlock
                    text: "Build #42: PASSED"
      out: updateResult
```

body:
## Problem

Jumping to a Warp-hosted session only activated the Warp app; with multiple windows or tabs open, the user still had to find the right one manually. Warp offered no way to target an existing tab or pane when this was last evaluated, which is why the README listed it under "Activates the app".

Warp has since shipped the missing mechanism: since [v0.2026.05.27](https://docs.warp.dev/changelog/2026), every terminal session exports `WARP_FOCUS_URL`, a deep link of the form `<channel-scheme>://session/<32 lowercase hex>` ([warpdotdev/warp#11130](https://github.com/warpdotdev/warp/pull/11130), closing the upstream request [warpdotdev/warp#8611](https://github.com/warpdotdev/warp/issues/8611)). Opening it makes Warp raise the owning window, switch to the tab, and focus the exact pane; a stale or unknown UUID is silently ignored.

Closes #229

## Solution

- `cctop-hook` captures `WARP_FOCUS_URL` at session start into a new optional `terminal.focus_url` field.
- Jump-to-session resolves Warp hosts to the existing `.openURL` strategy with activation-first ordering (`restoreAppAndOpenURL`), so the app still comes forward even when Warp ignores a stale UUID. Sessions without a captured link (older Warp, pre-update sessions) keep the previous activate-only behavior.
- `WarpFocusLink` validates the link against the exact shape `<scheme>://session/<32 hex>` with the scheme allowlisted to Warp's four release channels, and derives the activation bundle ID from the validated scheme (`warp` → `dev.warp.Warp-Stable`, `warppreview` → `dev.warp.Warp-Preview`, `warpdev` → `dev.warp.Warp-Dev`, `warposs` → `dev.warp.WarpOss`, per [warpdotdev/warp `script/macos/bundle`](https://github.com/warpdotdev/warp/blob/main/script/macos/bundle)). Validation runs both at capture and at focus time because session JSON is user-writable — a tampered file cannot make cctop open a non-Warp URL or activate a non-Warp bundle ID.
- README and site move Warp into the "Targets the exact session" tier, noting the required Warp version and the fallback.
- Two mechanical relocations keep strict SwiftLint green: the hook's terminal-capture helpers moved into an `extension HookHandler` (same file, mirroring the existing Cleanup extension), and `resolveRecentProjectOpenStrategy` moved to `FocusTerminal+Recent.swift` next to its main caller.

## Verification

- `make all` (swiftlint strict, hook contract validation, both builds, full test suite): 1185/1185 Swift tests pass plus the plugin suites.
- New tests: hook capture of a valid `WARP_FOCUS_URL` and rejection of a malformed one; strategy resolution for stable and preview channels, host detection via bundle ID when `TERM_PROGRAM` differs (tmux inside Warp), and a nine-URL tamper list (wrong scheme, uppercase scheme, uppercase hex, dashed UUID, extra path segments, query string, wrong host) all falling back to plain activation.
- Warp-side behavior was verified against Warp's open-source deep-link handler (`UriHost::Session` in `app/src/uri/mod.rs`) rather than a live install; Warp is not installed on this machine, so no end-to-end jump was exercised locally.

author: drakulavich
body:
Refs #685 — task 4.1. Blocking: this must land before any alpha is un-drafted.

## Why this is not cosmetic

Without it the alpha channel does not exist at the consumer end. `Resolve npm dist-tag` was:

```bash
if [[ "$version" == *-* ]]; then echo "tag=beta"
```

A CLI alpha (`1.27.0-alpha.1`) satisfies that branch and publishes to `@beta`. Everyone on `bun add -g @drakulavich/kesha-voice-kit@beta` — the install line documented in the `release-mechanics` skill — would silently start receiving alphas, and `npm view …@beta version` would stop meaning "the latest beta".

Un-drafting is the irreversible step, so this bites on the **first published alpha**, not in review.

## Change

Derive the tag from the SemVer prerelease identifier rather than from "has a hyphen":

| version | dist-tag |
| --- | --- |
| `1.27.0` | `latest` |
| `1.27.0-alpha.1` | `alpha` |
| `1.27.0-beta.2` | `beta` |
| `1.27.0-rc.1` | `rc` |

Generalises to any future channel with no further edit — strictly less code than adding an `alpha` special case beside the `beta` one.

## Two refusals instead of a silent surprise

- A version whose identifier decodes to `latest` (`1.27.0-latest.1`) is **rejected**. Publishing a prerelease there hands it to everyone who never asked for one.
- An identifier that is not a usable channel name (`1.27.0-1`, `1.27.0-Alpha.1`, `1.27.0-`) is **rejected** rather than silently becoming a dist-tag nobody meant to create.

## Why a script and not inline bash

The logic no longer fits CLAUDE.md's three-line limit for inline CI scripts. Extracting it also makes it unit-testable, which the inline bash was not.

Verified the refusal actually fails the workflow step, rather than being swallowed by command substitution — under `bash -e` as Actions runs it, a failing substitution in an assignment aborts the step:

```
$ bash -e -c 'tag=$(node .github/scripts/npm-dist-tag.mjs 1.27.0-latest.1); echo REACHED'
step exit=1          # REACHED never printed
```

## Verification

- `bun test` — 618 pass (7 new), 5 skip, 0 fail
- `bunx tsc --noEmit`, `bun run check:workflows`, `bun run check:release-manifest` — clean
- Exercised end to end the way the workflow calls it (no args → reads `package.json`)

## Still open on the alpha channel

Two things named in the #692 review, neither blocking this PR:

- The stable-engine-tag comparison against `package.json#version` already trips on `main` (CLI 1.27.0 vs engine 1.24.7) and must be settled **before the next stable engine release**.
- The alpha channel has no documented policy yet — the validators accept three shapes with no stated rule for choosing between them.

body:
## Summary

Adds `beets-nohirescd`, an independently packaged Beets plugin that prevents high-resolution source audio from being matched to MusicBrainz CD releases.

An album is considered high-resolution when any source track exceeds the configured bit-depth or sample-rate limit. CD candidates are removed before Beets makes an automatic or interactive selection.

## Import behavior

- Defaults to maximums of 16-bit and 44.1 kHz.
- Checks both album-level media and the media of mapped tracks.
- Handles mixed-media releases whose album media is represented as the generic `Media`.
- Matches CD variants including Enhanced CD, 8cm CD, SHM-CD, and CD-R.
- Deliberately excludes SACD.
- Filters initial candidates as well as candidates from manual searches and entered IDs.
- Recalculates Beets’ recommendation after filtering so quiet mode cannot retain a recommendation based on a removed candidate.

## Audit and reimport command

Adds:

```console
beet nohirescd [QUERY...]
beet nohirescd --output FILE [QUERY...]
beet nohirescd --reimport [QUERY...]
```

The default command audits stored album metadata without contacting MusicBrainz and prints a concise report.

`--output` additionally writes a UTF-8, album-level CSV containing:

- Beets and MusicBrainz album IDs
- Artist, album, path, and track count
- Maximum bit depth and sample rate
- Distinct stored media
- Aggregated high-resolution and CD track details

`--reimport` passes the exact violating album IDs to Beets’ library-reimport pipeline. It always uses album mode, restores the configured singleton setting afterward, and requires `import.autotag` so the candidate filter cannot be bypassed. Normal prompts and other import behavior remain intact.

Reimport can update library metadata and files according to the user’s Beets configuration.

## Packaging and documentation

- Adds the `beets-nohirescd` package at version `0.1.0`.
- Supports Python 3.10–3.14 and Beets 2.13 or newer.
- Adds plugin installation, configuration, audit, CSV, and reimport documentation.
- Adds the plugin to the repository index and development documentation.
- Adds Python-version compatibility CI and a dedicated Beets 2.13.0 minimum-version job.

#1361 taught `loop_detect` a third verdict and updated the doc comments on `AgentEvent::LoopDetected`'s `kind`, `pattern` and `repeats` to mention it. The exported contract is generated **from those doc comments**, so editing the prose alone leaves `docs/wire/` stale. Fix is `make wire-schema-update` and nothing else.

## The contract does not move

This is the part worth checking rather than taking on trust, so I checked it mechanically. Every changed line across all four artifacts is a `description` string or its `.d.ts` comment twin:

```
-   * `"exact_repeat"` | `"short_cycle"` — mirrors
+   * `"exact_repeat"` | `"short_cycle"` | `"stagnation"` — mirrors
```

Filtering the diff for `"type"`, `"const"`, `"required"`, `"properties"`, `"items"`, `"format"`, `"minimum"`, `"$ref"` returns **nothing**. No field is added, removed, renamed, or made required.

So this is not even the *additive* case the wire rule is written to permit — it is structurally a no-op. No `--output-format stream-json` consumer, SSE consumer, or `agentevent.d.ts` user can observe it.

## The witness

- [x] The guard **is** the witness: `check-wire-schema.sh` fails on `main` and passes here.

Second wire staleness in two hours, and the two have *different* causes: #1347 went stale by adding a `ServerFrame` variant, #1361 by editing a sentence. Because the artifacts are generated from doc comments, "I only touched a comment" is not a safe assumption — which is exactly why it slips through.

`wire-schema` also runs only in `make gate` and the pre-push hook. Anyone merging with an admin override or a stale local hook lands this without seeing it, which AGENTS.md already records happening at #1185.

body:
## Gaps by namespace — the chart was not the problem

On real data the section rendered **eleven segments of 8% each**, under an eleven-entry legend of 60-character namespaces. A stacked bar shows *dominance*; eleven equal slivers show nothing.

But the cause was upstream of the chart. Run-scoped namespaces carry the run id:

    af10fde4-94d9-49fb-897f-b9b7f2423382:noxys-developer:developer
    02e8acdf-08aa-40ae-ba68-a370bba64624:noxys-developer:developer
    df1beab0-a436-4cf7-99ed-ef28bebfbadc:noxys-developer:developer
    209a6fd7-4eaf-4b9f-acb4-90eba8b6c7c4:noxys-developer:developer

Every run mints a **new** namespace, so the same role can never accumulate — four `noxys-developer` gaps appeared as four separate 1-gap entries, and no trend could ever form no matter how the data was drawn.

Gaps are now grouped by scope with the leading run id stripped, and ranked as a list. Those four collapse into one row with 4 gaps, and a ranking finally exists.

**Only a leading UUID is removed.** `noxys:noxys-cto-review:cto` keeps its `noxys` prefix — that is a project, not a run, and stripping by *position* rather than by *shape* would merge namespaces that are genuinely distinct.

**A scope seen across several runs says so** ("across 4 runs"). A gap that recurs run after run is a different problem from one that happened once, and the count alone cannot tell them apart.

## Partitions — say what it is before how it works

The read-only copy opened with the mechanism — *"Ratifying a partition — the single gate between a proposal and N running agents — needs an approve-rank token"* — before ever saying what a partition is.

It now leads with the thing itself: **a plan split into tasks, proposed by an agent, that a human ratifies before any of it runs.** The empty state says what would produce one rather than only quoting the command's syntax.

## Verification

678 web tests (10 new: the grouping helper in isolation, plus a view test asserting four run-scoped namespaces collapse to one row and the run ids never reach the label). Plus `tsc`, `oxlint`, and the committed bundle rebuilt.

body:
Both regressions bisect to 2e323599 (#419) and together broke the embedding plugin end to end: a 17.2 GB scratch OOM at engine boot on ≤16 GB cards, and silently garbage embeddings on cards where the slab fit. Diagnosed on the local RTX 4080 via `tests/serving/test_vllm_plugin_gpu.py::test_vllm_plugin_embed_matches_hf_eager`.

## Bug 1 — flash P@V deferral false positive materializes every o_proj product

`010_merge_loop_ops`'s `_sum_contracts_exp_producer` scanned **every** other operand of a sum-contraction for an exp within one producer hop. A residual add whose reduce half already merged in sits within two hops of the previous layer's silu sigmoid (or softmax), so the guard classified every o_proj residual add past layer 0 as a "future flash P@V offer site" and refused the product/reduce halves-merge — the decomposed product stayed materialized as a `(b, s, k, n)` f16 gmem scratch per layer (17.2 GB at S=4096 on the Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B trunk). Layer 0 escaped only because its residual is the embedding.

Fix: only operands whose loads feed the add-`Accum` (a backward dataflow closure, `_accum_feed_names`) get the exp scan; post-reduce epilogue operands are exempt. The true positive — P@V with its softmax mid-assembly, where the exp-adjacent operand feeds the accumulate — still defers (covered by a new test).

## Bug 2 — kernel names blind to buffer dtypes alias f16/f32 twins

`provenance.name_for`'s 6-hex suffix hashed only `body.structural_key()`, which carries no buffer decls. With bug 1 fixed (and pre-fix at smaller S), the last layer's down_proj+residual fuses into the final norm's **f32** cast — algebraically identical to the per-layer **f16** `add_NN` twin — so both hashed to one name, and `plan_from_graph`'s per-name kernel dedup ("first source wins", a debug-level log) handed the f32 node the f16 cubin. The buffer then held f16 byte pairs read as f32: layers 0–26 bit-perfect, final layer garbage (reinterpreting the buffer as contiguous f16 gives cosine +1.0000 vs torch).

Fix: `name_for_loop` threads an io dtype signature from the graph decls into the name hash, restoring the documented contract that distinct kernels never share a name. All kernel-name hash suffixes change, so the cubin cache recompiles once; goldens and the tune DB are keyed by row spelling / op digest, not names, and are unaffected.

## Validation

- `test_vllm_plugin_embed_matches_hf_eager` passes again on the RTX 4080 (was: cupy OOM allocating 17,205,035,008 bytes)
- Runner probe vs HF eager at S=256: last-token cosine 0.99999 (was 0.00)
- Full suite: 2824 passed, 159 skipped; attention/flash e2e coverage green; lint clean
- New regression tests: fixpoint + guard-level (fail pre-fix) in `test_fusion_rules.py`, dtype-naming in `test_loop_naming.py`

Also worth noting for a follow-up: the same collision class exists in `op_cache_key` (term/knob keys carry no output dtype), which can conflate f16/f32 twins' tune-DB evidence — a perf-evidence issue, not correctness, left out of this PR to avoid invalidating existing DB keyings.

Task2/3/4 の Desktop relay 実装が既存の契約を3点回帰させていた。当時 bats が未導入で気付かれていない（`task-3-report.md` に記載あり）。実装側のみ修正、テストは一切変更していない。

- **app-server の正常終了をブリッジの失敗にしていた** — `onDisconnect` が exit code を見ずに常に exit 1。`exit 0` での正常終了もエラー扱いになっていた（test 45 / 48）。
- **#276 の resume フォールバックが広すぎた** — 「resume は成功したが別のスレッドIDが返った」ケースまで飲み込んでおり、他人のスレッドへ wake を中継しうる状態だった。本家と同じく全モードで fail closed に戻した（test 47）。
- **idle watchdog が生きている turn を打ち切っていた** — stale 判定が `turnGeneration` ベースだったため、turn id を返さない app-server では2周目以降の完了通知が全て stale として捨てられ、watchdog 経由でしか turn が終わらなくなっていた。「終了通知が未回収の turn 数」を数える方式に置き換えた（test 58 / 59）。

### macOS 固有の失敗（約30件・原因は4つ）

本家 `fujibee/agmsg` main の macOS shard は緑で、これらは**このフォークが持ち込んだもの**。同一 runner イメージ（bash 3.2.57 / sqlite3 3.50.6 と ubuntu の bash 5.2 / sqlite3 3.45.1）。

| 原因 | 件数 | 修正 |
|---|---|---|
| `agmsg_sqlite_mem` に `-escape off` が渡っておらず、sqlite ≥3.50 で `char(31)` 区切りが文字列 `^_` になり全メッセージが `[] : ` になる | 8 | `scripts/lib/storage.sh` |
| fork 専用 fixture の `mapfile`（bash 4.0+、`-d` は 4.4+）が macOS の bash 3.2 で存在せず、args が空のままブリッジが起動 | 20 | `tests/fixtures/codex_task3.sh` |
| handoff JSON エスケープの BSD sed 非互換 | 1 | `scripts/lib/codex-app-server.sh` |
| `set -u` + bash <4.4 で空配列の `"${arr[@]}"` が unbound になる | 潜在 | `scripts/check-inbox.sh` |
| 固定 sleep のウォッチャヘルパ（フレーク、本家が既に修正済み） | 2 | `tests/test_watch.bats` を本家版に差し替え |

sed の件は落ちていたテストが示すより壊れていた。ラベルを `-e` で分けても BSD sed は最終行の `N` で何も出力せず終了する（pattern space を出力するのは GNU だけ）ため、**単一行の値——ここでは通常のケース——が空になる**。加えて slurp 前にバックスラッシュ・引用符の置換を実行していたので2行目以降は未エスケープだった。sed をやめて bash のパターン置換にした。

## レビュー対応（敵対的レビューの指摘）

- **遅延通知の記憶が失効しなかった** — `unreportedTurnEnds` 整数カウンタに3つの欠陥（idle 中に届いた通知で決済されない / watchdog 経由でも加算するため上限なく累積する / `queueTurnEnded` の同世代 dedup が `reported=true` を捨てる）。「直前に終了通知を回収せず終わった turn」1件だけを generation と id で覚えるスロットに置き換え、ターン終了ごとに無条件上書きして1境界を越えないようにした。
- **`cleanExit` が bridge の状態を見ていなかった** — desktop では `turn/start` 直後に claim を `delivered` で ack するため、その後 app-server が exit 0 すると「メッセージは消費済み・実作業なし・exit 0 で成功報告」になっていた。静止状態（turn なし・pending wake なし・未 ack claim なし）でゲートする。
- **escape フラグの IFS 依存** — 未クォートの `$_AGMSG_ESCAPE_FLAG` は `$IFS` で分割されるため、IFS に空白を含まない呼び出し元（`check-inbox.sh` は `IFS=$'\x1f'` / `IFS=','` にする）からは1引数として渡り `unknown option` になる。配列で保持するようにした。
- **カバレッジの穴** — レビューが「`currentTurnFromParams` を旧ルール（`turnGeneration > 1`）に戻しても既存の id なしテスト3件が通る」ことを実証した（fake app-server が id なし完了を `turnNumber === 1` でしか出さないため）。旧ルールでも壊れたカウンタでも落ち、修正版でのみ通るテストを2件追加し、両方向で判別できることを確認した。

## 残り

このPRの範囲外として issue に切り出した。

- #10 — `claim_barrier` が `check-inbox.sh` 経由で発火しない（原因未特定。本家マージ後はテストだけ通り、バリア自体は死んだまま）
- #11 — `_agmsg_codex_json_escape` が `\n \r \t` 以外の制御バイトを素通しし、handoff が無診断で失われる（旧 sed 版も同じなので回帰ではない）
- #12 — escape flag の probe がコマンド置換で毎回走り、sqlite3 が呼び出しあたり2プロセスになる（実測。Stop フックのホットパス）

`test_codex_bridge_launcher.bats` のフレーク (#6) は未着手。

## CI

全14チェック green。macOS 1/4 が一度 `Error: in prepare, database is locked (5)` で落ちてジョブが25分ハングしたが、同一コミットの再実行で緑になったためフレーク（本家 #595「main 自体が約半分の実行で落ち、落ちるテストは毎回違う」と同じ症状）。

## ローカル検証（Linux/WSL）

`test_codex_bridge` 66/0（レビュー対応で追加した2件を含む）、`test_delivery` 147/0、`test_storage` 18/0、`test_inbox` 12/0、`test_codex_monitor` 10/0、`test_dispatch` 7/0。

`test_watch` はこの環境で4件落ちるが、うち3件は**修正前のテストファイルでも同じように落ち**、CI では全て pass するため、このマシン固有の事象として切り分けた。

author: copilot
body:
This introduces the core control plane for short-lived secure document sharing: private-storage-only shares, app-mediated recipient verification, one-hour expiry, and short-lived download issuance after successful email/password/OTP validation. It models the required AWS pattern without exposing raw S3 presigned URLs as the primary access path.

- **Share session lifecycle**
  - Added a minimal share service to create expiring share sessions with:
    - recipient email normalization and hashing
    - one-time password generation
    - salted password hashing at rest
    - file manifest and audit log capture
    - scheduled cleanup metadata for hard 1-hour expiry
  - Sessions are denied once expired and can be explicitly expired for object/metadata cleanup.

- **Recipient-bound access controls**
  - Added recipient validation flow requiring:
    - exact intended email
    - generated password
    - one-time verification code
  - Prevents bearer-link-only access by gating download authorization behind application validation.

- **Upload/download orchestration**
  - Added upload URL generation primitives that enforce encrypted upload headers (`SSE-KMS`).
  - Added download authorization that returns a short-lived ZIP download reference instead of exposing multiple raw object URLs.
  - Enforced single-download behavior by default.

- **Minimal integration surface**
  - Added lightweight API entry points that can be wired to Lambda handlers or another web layer without changing core logic.
  - Kept persistence, mail, scheduling, and storage adapters abstracted behind small interfaces for later AWS integration.

- **Docs and focused test coverage**
  - Updated the repository README to describe the security model and module layout.
  - Added focused tests for:
    - 1-hour expiry
    - hashed password storage
    - recipient + password + OTP gating
    - single-download enforcement

Example:

```python
share = service.create_share(
    recipient_email="recipient@example.com",
    files=[{"path": "folder/file.txt", "size_bytes": 12, "content_type": "text/plain"}],
)

service.request_otp(
    share_id=share["shareId"],
    recipient_email="recipient@example.com",
    ******"password"],
)

download = service.authorize_download(
    share_id=share["shareId"],
    recipient_email="recipient@example.com",
    ******"password"],
    otp_code=otp_code,
)
```

<!-- START COPILOT CODING AGENT SUFFIX -->



<!-- START COPILOT ORIGINAL PROMPT -->



<details>

<summary>Original prompt</summary>

1-hour secure document share on AWS
1. Core pattern

Use a private S3 bucket as the storage layer, but never expose it publicly. AWS states that S3 objects are private by default and that presigned URLs can grant time-limited access to download objects.

The secure flow should be:

Uploader signs in to your web app.
Uploader selects a folder.
App creates a share session with:
recipient email address
expiry time: 1 hour
generated strong password
folder/object manifest
audit metadata
Browser uploads files directly to S3 using short-lived presigned PUT or POST URLs.
Recipient receives a notification email with a secure access page link.
Recipient must enter:
their email address
the generated password
ideally a one-time email code or magic-link verification
Only after validation does the backend generate short-lived download URLs or a temporary ZIP bundle.
At the 1-hour expiry, the app disables access and deletes the S3 objects, metadata and secret material.

AWS describes presigned URLs as signed requests with an explicit X-Amz-Expires parameter, where the allowed action still depends on the IAM credentials and policies used to generate the URL.

Important design correction: “specific email address” access

A presigned S3 URL is effectively a bearer token. Anyone who has the URL can use it until it expires, unless you put another control in front of it. AWS describes presigned URLs as granting time-limited permission, but the URL itself can be entered in a browser or used by a program to download the object.

So, if you want access limited to a specific email address, do not send a raw S3 presigned URL as the primary access mechanism. Instead:

Send the recipient a link to your application.
Require the recipient to prove control of the target email address.
Require the generated password.
Only then generate a very short-lived download URL or stream the ZIP via the application.

This gives you email-bound access, rather than just link possession access.

Proposed AWS components
Capability	AWS service	PurposeWeb/API entry point	Amazon CloudFront, AWS WAF, API Gateway	HTTPS access, rate limiting, request protection
Upload/download orchestration	AWS Lambda or ECS Fargate	Create share sessions, validate recipient, issue presigned URLs
Temporary file storage	Amazon S3	Private encrypted storage for uploaded documents
Encryption keys	AWS KMS	Customer-managed key for S3 object encryption
Secret/password generation	AWS Secrets Manager	Generate strong password or secret material
Metadata/session store	DynamoDB	Share ID, recipient email hash, expiry, object manifest, status
Email notification	Amazon SES, or corporate email workflow	Notify recipient without attaching files
Cleanup	EventBridge Scheduler + Lambda	Delete objects and revoke share session after 1 hour
Audit/security monitoring	CloudTrail, CloudWatch, GuardDuty, Security Hub, AWS Config	Audit access, detect suspicious behaviour, monitor configuration

AWS Secrets Manager supports generating passwords through CloudFormation, AWS CLI and AWS SDKs. The internal Employee Document Management Security Overview v1.7.pdf also describes an AWS pattern using CloudTrail, AWS Config, Security Hub, GuardDuty, Trusted Advisor, KMS, Secrets Manager and transient storage with deletion after processing.

Secure flow in more detail
A. Upload flow
Uploader authenticates to the service.
Uploader provides the recipient email address.
Backend creates a shareId.
Backend generates a strong one-time password using AWS Secrets Manager.
Backend stores only a hashed password, not the plaintext password, in DynamoDB.
Backend returns the password to the uploader once.
Backend issues short-lived presigned upload URLs for each file.
Browser uploads directly to S3 over HTTPS.

The AWS Security Blog describes S3 presigned URLs as an AWS file-sharing option with time-limited URLs, IAM controls for URL generation and HTTPS.

B. Recipient access flow
Recipient opens the access page.
Recipient enters their email and password.
App sends a one-time verification code to the expected email address.
Recipient enters the one-time code.
Backend checks:
share has not expired
email matches the intended recipient
password hash matches
OTP/magic-link verification passed
download count, if you choose to limit it
Backend generates a short-lived download URL or produces a temporary ZIP for the folder.
C. Expiry and deletion flow

S3 Lifecycle is useful for object lifecycle management and expiration, but it is not the right primary mechanism for a precise 1-hour expiry because lifecycle policies are generally age-based lifecycle rules rather than per-share application timers. AWS describes lifecycle expiration as deleting objects at the end of their lifetime based on lifecycle configuration.

For this use case, use:

Application-level expiry: deny access after 1 hour.
EventBridge Scheduler: schedule a one-time cleanup event for each share.
Cleanup Lambda: delete S3 objects, delete temporary ZIPs, delete Secrets...

</details>

author: souliane
body:
`MachineSignal.ram_available_gb` was declared and populated by nothing. All four production callers of `read_machine_signal` pass no argument (`loop/admission.py:103`, `core/dispatch_admission.py:65`, `core/headless_admission.py:233`, `hooks/scripts/resume_admission.py:93`), so the field was `None` on every live call and the governor sized concurrency on cores and load alone.

`cores * 2` is 16 xdist workers on an 8-core box: 10.4 GB at the measured p50 worker RSS, **19.8 GB at the p90 against 19.7 GB usable**. Safe at the median, over the line at the tail — which is the whole shape of the intermittent-but-relentless OOM.

## The formula in the issue is wrong, and this PR does not implement it

The issue proposes `per_agent_test_workers = min(cpu_bound, floor(ram_available_gb / 1.25))`. That is dimensionally inconsistent: `cpu_bound` is already **per-agent** (`total // active_agents`) while `floor(ram / 1.25)` is **box-wide**. With four agents each would be granted the whole box budget — a 4x over-admission, so the OOM fix would itself over-admit.

The RAM term therefore bounds the **TOTAL**, and the per-agent share is taken after:

```python
total = max(1, int(cores)) * TOTAL_TEST_WORKERS_PER_CORE
if ram_available_gb is not None and per_worker_gb > 0:
    total = min(total, math.floor(max(0.0, ram_available_gb - RAM_BRAKE_FLOOR_GB) / per_worker_gb))
return max(1, total // max(1, int(active_agents)))
```

## What changed

Two-sided, because the field had no producer either.

**Producer.** `read_machine_signal` populates the reading from `teatree.utils.ram_probe.effective_available_ram_mib` — the one cgroup-aware reader (`min(host MemAvailable, memory.max - memory.current)`). No hand-rolled `/proc/meminfo` read: inside a container that reports the HOST figure, and a second reader would be invisible to [#4118](https://github.com/souliane/teatree/issues/4118)'s fix. Its `None` (unreadable) stays a different answer from `0` (nothing left). An explicit argument still wins.

**Consumers — three, and deliberately not a fourth.**

- `per_agent_test_workers` — the bound above.
- `_machine_brake` — a RAM watermark beside the load one (`RAM_BRAKE_FLOOR_GB = 4.0`, `RAM_RESUME_FLOOR_GB = 6.0`), so it inherits that brake's hysteresis and its cheap-lane exemption for free.
- `resume_agent_ceiling` — scales by `min(load headroom, memory headroom)`. The recorded restore ([#4108](https://github.com/souliane/teatree/issues/4108)) was load 58 **and** 1 GB free; a bound reading only load calls that half healthy. The memory term is inert above the upper watermark, so it lowers the ceiling only on a genuinely tight box.

It is **not** a term in `_machine_ceiling` / `_adaptive_ceiling`. `adapt_concurrency` already owns "how many agents fit in memory", and two unsynchronised readers of one quantity drift ([#4125](https://github.com/souliane/teatree/issues/4125)). A brake answers a different question.

**Fail-safe is BOUNDED, not closed** — [#4101](https://github.com/souliane/teatree/issues/4101) restated. An unreadable probe (or a non-positive per-worker size) yields exactly today's CPU-derived bound, the brake does not fire, and resume stays load-derived. Never a denial and never a manufactured clamp to 1: denying on an unreadable `/proc` file is a kill switch operated by a missing file.

**The p90 is a setting, not a magic number.** `test_worker_ram_gb` (`UserSettings`, DB-home, per-overlay overridable, default **1.25**), derived from the kernel OOM log 2026-07-21..08-04: p50 0.65 / p90 1.24 / max 23.1 GB. The p90 is the sizing point; the max is one pathological run, not a budget. The derivation is recorded in the settings comment. The pure function reads no config — `with_test_worker_cap` resolves the setting and passes it in.

## RED first

The behavioural RED, on the seam that reaches the child (`with_test_worker_cap` → `PYTEST_XDIST_AUTO_NUM_WORKERS`), observed on the pre-fix code — an **equality** failure, not a TypeError:

```
FAILED tests/teatree_core/test_admission_governor.py::TestTheExportedCapRespondsToMemory::
  test_a_memory_tight_box_exports_fewer_workers_than_a_roomy_one - assert 16 < 16
```

40 GB and 6 GB both produced 16. After the change: 16 and 1.

Also RED-then-green: the pure bound falling with the reading, `ram_available_gb=None` returning exactly today's CPU bound (4, not 1, not 0), the total bound holding across the agent range, a 1 GB box still getting one worker, the brake naming its reading, `None` admitting, a braked governor held to the higher floor, the cheap lane skipping the RAM brake as it skips load, and the resume ceiling's three cases. `TestUnreadableProbeNeverManufacturesAClamp` and `test_an_eight_core_box_admits_four` are untouched and green.

One existing test moved rather than broke: `tests/teatree_loop/test_admission.py::TestMachineSignal` asserted `ram_available_gb is None` on the default path. That assertion pinned the defect — it now asserts the field is populated from the probe.

## Trade-off stated rather than left silent

**The cheap lane is exempt from the RAM brake while still consuming memory.** The exemption ([#4098](https://github.com/souliane/teatree/issues/4098)) is what stops the work-retiring phases being refused on the load their expensive siblings created, and folding memory into `_machine_brake` inherits it. The judgement here is that the bound is sufficient — the cheap lane is capped at 2 seats, and the worker cap is **not** exempt, so a cheap agent's own suite is still sized on live memory. A reviewer should re-derive that rather than take it on trust: two cheap agents at the p90 total 2.5 GB of workers plus their own footprint, against a 4 GB brake floor.

## Known argued NON-change

`_headless_env.py` used `os.cpu_count()` (host 8) rather than `available_cpu_count()` (cgroup 7). That is a real divergence, but fixing it here would shift the CPU bound on a different axis inside the same diff and make any fallout un-attributable. The CPU term is preserved byte-for-byte: `with_test_worker_cap` now reads `machine.cores` from `read_machine_signal`, which is itself `os.cpu_count() or 1`. Worth its own issue.

## Live reading on the box at implementation time

`effective_available_ram_mib() = 17461 MiB → 17.05 GB` (host `MemAvailable`; no cgroup v2 limit visible from the host). Well clear of `RAM_BRAKE_FLOOR_GB = 4.0`, so the brake does **not** fire on merge. In the container the same probe sees the worker's cgroup limit instead, which is the point of using it.

## Test result

- `tests/teatree_core` + `tests/teatree_loop` + `tests/teatree_utils`: **14461 passed, 17 skipped** (28m50s, `PYTEST_XDIST_AUTO_NUM_WORKERS=4`)
- `tests/teatree_core/test_admission_governor.py` + `tests/config`: **1929 passed**
- `tests/conformance` + headless/dispatch admission + resume hook + gate-liveness corpus + `tests/teatree_agents`: **1778 passed** (with the one pinned-defect assertion since updated)
- `uv run tach check`: all modules validated
- `uv run ruff check src tests`: clean

The diff-scoped lane escalates to FULL on the `defaults.toml` change (`toolchain/config is un-modellable`), so the directly-reachable suites were run instead of a 34k-test sweep on a memory-tight host. CI's sharded lane remains the authority.

## Architecture pre-check — #4163

**1. BLUEPRINT § alignment** — § 272 (adaptive admission governor). Updated in this PR with the memory term, the three consumers, the non-consumers and why, the fail-safe table, the setting, and the cheap-lane trade-off.

**2. FSM phase boundaries** — n/a. No `Ticket.State` / `Worktree.State` transition.

**3. Extension-point contracts** — n/a. No `OverlayBase` hook, scanner registration, or `*Backend` Protocol. `per_agent_test_workers` keeps its name and its caller, so `tests/conformance/test_consumer_caller_walk.py` still enrols the consumer.

**4. Component boundaries** — the whole production change is `core/admission_governor.py` (the pure decision) plus the one-line-per-argume

author: abkfenris
body:
Renovate rewrites the dependency spec in `pyproject.toml` and leaves `pixi.lock` alone. `setup-pixi` then runs `pixi install --locked`, which rejects the workspace and kills the e2e job ten seconds in, before any test runs:

```
Error: × lock file not up-to-date with the workspace
```

## Why it looks intermittent

Only bumps that move *outside* the already-locked version break:

| PR | spec change | locked | satisfies? |
|----|-------------|--------|-----------|
| #109 | `fastapi >=0.139,<0.140` → `>=0.140,<0.141` | `0.139.0` | no → fails in 10s |
| #88 | `playwright >=1.49,<1.61` → `>=1.62,<1.63` | `1.60.0` | no → fails in 10s |
| #97 | `numpy <2.5.1` → `<2.5.2` | `2.5.0` | yes → suite runs |

## The workflow

On push to `renovate/**`: regenerate the lock, commit it back to the branch, then ask `Push` to run against the new commit.

That last step is **not optional**. A push made with `GITHUB_TOKEN` does not trigger `on: push`, so without the explicit dispatch the PR head would move to a commit carrying *no checks at all* — worse than a red one. The same mechanic is why this cannot loop on its own commit, so no `github.actor` guard is needed (which also keeps zizmor's `bot-conditions` audit out of the picture).

Other details:

- `setup-pixi` runs with `run-install: false`, since its default `pixi install --locked` is precisely what a stale lock breaks.
- `contents: write` to push, `actions: write` to dispatch, both scoped to this one job.
- This is the only workflow here that keeps checkout credentials instead of `persist-credentials: false`, because it has to push. Worth knowing: `artipacked` does flag that at zizmor's `auditor` persona (Low confidence) but not at the `pedantic` persona this repo runs, so no inline ignore is needed.
- If `pixi lock` cannot resolve a bump — note `exclude-newer = "7d"` in `[tool.pixi.workspace]` and the existing comment about it splitting the playwright driver/library pair — the job fails loudly on that branch, which is the signal you want instead of a silently stale lock.

## Verification

Validated locally against the repo's own hooks: `zizmor --offline --persona=pedantic` reports no findings across all three workflows, `check-jsonschema --builtin-schema vendor.github-workflows` passes, and `prettier --prose-wrap=always --check` is clean.

The workflow itself cannot run until it is on `main`. After merge, trigger it via `workflow_dispatch` against `renovate/fastapi-0.x`: expect a lock commit moving `fastapi-0.139.0` → `0.140.x`, a dispatched `Push` run on that ref, and #109 going green. Then repeat for `renovate/playwright-monorepo` (#88).

author: ljosberinn
body:
Closes the hole phase 27 named: every e2e spec ran against an **empty** library, so nothing had ever looked at a row — and the row is where the defects land. The first of the three that shipped was the playing marker drawn in `--accent` on a row *filled* with `--accent`.

## Getting music in

`Add Folder…` opens the OS folder picker, which WebDriver cannot answer, so `add_watch_folder` is the one command the test drives itself through `window.__TAURI__`. After that it is the app's own path: click **Rescan**, which scans and refreshes exactly as it does for a user.

The mp3s are generated in Node at spec time — silent MPEG-1 frames behind a hand-written ID3v2.3 tag, no dependency — the same trade `src-tauri/tests/fixture` already makes: no encoder, no binary blobs in git, no licensing question about the audio. Verified against the real scanner before being wired up: 6 added, the `.jpg` and `.txt` ignored, every tag read back, durations distinct and mid-second.

Six tracks over three artists, chosen so title order and artist order interleave differently — a sort assertion that held under both would prove nothing.

## Playing anything

A runner has no audio device, so the app falls back to `NullSink`, where every load fails **by design**. No row could ever be marked playing. `SilentSink` accepts a load and advances position on a wall clock; it never reports itself finished, so the queue cannot advance mid-assertion.

## Isolation

`PLAYER_E2E_DATA_DIR` gives each spec file its own library — otherwise this spec's six tracks break the spec that asserts on an empty one, and on a developer's machine it would be *their* library. The seeded spec asserts the empty state **before** it writes anything, so an override that stopped being honoured fails as itself rather than as a wrong row count.

Both variables are read only by a build carrying the `wdio` feature, so a shipped binary cannot be pointed at another library or handed a fake audio device.

## What the rows are now asserted to do

- carry what the scanner read — whole rows at once, so a shifted column is legible in the failure
- count six, and leave the two non-audio files alone
- sort both ways
- extend a selection with shift
- mark the row being played, and name it in the status display
- **keep the playing marker at 3:1 both on the selected row and off it, and every row's text at 4.5:1 — in both themes**

## Cost

One more app launch on a job that already builds the binary, plus a scan of six ~100 kB files. Nothing added to storage: fixtures are written under `e2e/.tmp`, gitignored and rebuilt per run.

## **Description**

  Turning notifications off for all wallet-activity accounts and then turning a single account back on re-enabled notifications for **every** account.

  Root cause: "Deselect all" performs two writes. The first (`toggleAllAccounts`) disables every account in the preferences blob via the controller. The second flips the wallet-activity push/in-app channels by
  writing the whole `walletActivity` section — and it built that section by spreading `preferences.walletActivity` captured in the render closure, i.e. the pre-toggle copy where every account was still enabled.
  That second write replaced the blob wholesale and undid the first. The screen showed the accounts as off because presence data was not refetched, so the corruption only surfaced on the next refetch — after
  enabling one account, every switch turned on.

  Fix:
  - `NotificationSettingsSection.tsx` — the toggle-all channel write now uses the updater form of `updatePreferencesSection`, so the section is derived from the latest preferences instead of the render-time copy.
  Also removes the now-redundant `preferences` guard and dependency.
  - `AccountsList.hooks.tsx` — `refetchAccountSettings` now refreshes the cached preferences blob alongside presence data. Account enable/disable is written by the controller behind that cache, so without this any
  later section write (a channel toggle after changing accounts) would persist a stale `accounts` array and resurrect the accounts the user just changed.

author: tamada
body:
Closes #32.

> **Stacked on #31.** Its branch is the base, because this rewrites the
> Visibility Control section #31 just corrected. Retarget to `main` once #31
> lands; the diff shown here will shrink to this commit alone.

## The problem

`$emit` decides only what the node it appears on emits. A sub-path with no
`$emit` of its own emits everything, so this publishes the full dataset one
level down despite the empty `$emit`:

```json
{ "staff": { "$emit": [], "by-name": {} } }
```

```
dist/staff/by-name/index.json      <- every record, salary included
dist/staff/by-name/1/index.json
dist/staff/by-name/2/index.json
```

`by-name` carries no directives at all. The exposure also appears late: the
config is correct when written, and becomes wrong when someone adds a sub-path
under a node they did not know was meant to stay unpublished.

## The fix

`$skip: true` leaves the node **and everything beneath it** ungenerated.
`materialize_node` returns before reading data and before looking at sub-paths,
so a skipped subtree is never visited.

That is what makes the requirement structural rather than a convention:
**nothing below can publish, because nothing below is read.** Verified for each
way of trying to get through:

| attempt | result |
|---|---|
| sub-path with no directives | withheld |
| sub-path with an explicit `$emit: ["list"]` | withheld |
| descendant setting `$skip: false` | withheld |
| grandchild that emits | withheld |
| template sub-path (`${name}` + `$derive`) | withheld |

Nothing under the node reaches the discovery index either.

`$skip` is not inherited as a value — it is the point the walk stops at. So
`$skip` on a sub-path withholds that subtree and leaves its ancestors
emitting, which is covered by its own test.

## On the name

Earlier documentation described a `$private` doing this. It was never
implemented — `ApiNode` collects unknown keys through `#[serde(flatten)]`, so
`"$private": true` was rejected as a sub-path of the wrong type. Since it never
worked, there is no compatibility cost to a different name, and `$skip` is the
better one: it says what happens to the build. Nothing is generated, which is
not the same as generating something and protecting it — static hosting has no
access control, and neither does this tool. `$private` remains rejected.

## Verification

- `just pre-push` passes: clippy clean, `cargo fmt --all --check` clean,
  27 unit + 49 integration + 13 doc tests green.
- Four regression tests added, including the override table above as a
  parameterised case.
- Both documented examples were run and produce exactly what the text claims.

## Found while doing this

A misspelled directive silently becomes an endpoint named after the typo
(`{"users": {"$fliter": {}}}` generates `/users/$fliter`). Pre-existing, not
from this change; filed as #34.

body:
Dernier morceau du modèle Otami relevé le 04/08 en lecture seule : **sa liste est une liste de FORMATS, pas de recettes** — nom du format en gras, recette mère en italique dessous. Ses « 409 fiches » sont 409 formats.

PILOTE affichait encore une ligne par fiche, résumant le format **par défaut**, avec une chip « N formats » qui ne servait qu'à dire ce que la liste ne montrait pas. Conséquence concrète : un boucher qui vend le même produit à la pièce **et** au kilo ne voyait qu'un des deux prix — et donc qu'une des deux marges — dans l'écran qu'il balaye justement pour repérer ce qui ne marge pas.

## Ce que ça change

- **Une ligne = un format de vente.** `ListeRecipe` devient `ListeLigne` (`{ key, recipeId, formatId, nom, recetteNom, … }`). Le nom en gras est celui du **format**, l'italique rappelle la **recette mère** — et seulement quand le format porte un autre nom qu'elle (toute fiche naît avec un format à son propre nom : le répéter n'apprendrait rien). Le rendement par batch reste en second segment.
- **Rien n'est recalculé.** Le coût du batch est commun à tous les formats (même fabrication) ; la partie *vente* de chaque ligne est le verdict que le serveur produit déjà avec `computeFormatVerdict`. `coutUniteAffiche` / `verdictAffiche` appellent toujours `venteQty` et `margeEtCoef` du moteur — un seul moteur, aucune donnée dérivée stockée.
- **La chip « N formats » disparaît.**
- **Coche verte** sur les formats validés (reprise d'Otami), devant le nom.
- **Ouvrir une ligne ouvre la fiche SUR CE FORMAT** : nouvelle prop `initialFormatId` du `FichePanel`, et lien direct `?format=<id>` sur `/dashboard/recettes/[id]` (lu sans `useSearchParams`, qui imposerait une frontière Suspense à la page).
- **Tri, interrupteur main-d'œuvre, cibles de marge, « À retravailler »** opèrent sur les lignes. À valeur égale, les formats d'une même fiche restent groupés et dans leur ordre — deux lignes qui parlent de la même fabrication se lisent l'une sous l'autre. Les valeurs absentes partent toujours en dernier, dans les deux sens.
- **Recherche** : les formats sont cherchés par nom de format, nom de recette, catégorie et ingrédients ; la liste déroulante affiche le format et sa recette mère, et le clic ouvre le bon format.

## Ce que comptent les compteurs — et c'est écrit à l'écran

L'unité de compte devient le **format**, parce que c'est le format qui porte un prix, donc une marge : une fiche vendue en deux conditionnements peut très bien tenir sa cible sur l'un et pas sur l'autre.

- KPI « **Formats de vente** » : le nombre de formats, avec « sur N fiches » juste dessous — sans ce rappel, « 12 » sur 9 fiches se lirait comme 12 produits.
- Chips de catégorie : « **Tous les formats (N)** » et un compte de formats par catégorie.
- En-tête de section : « N **formats** ».
- « À retravailler » : « N **formats** sous la cible de marge de sa catégorie — le plus bas d'abord ».
- Marge moyenne : « sur N **formats** chiffrés ».
- « Prix manquants » reste un compte de **fiches** — un ingrédient sans prix est un défaut de la fiche, pas d'un format — et le libellé le dit.

## Garde-fous

- Fiche sans aucun format (ne devrait plus exister depuis la reprise du lot 46) : elle apparaît quand même, avec les champs de vente que l'API renvoie déjà. Une fiche absente de sa propre liste serait pire qu'une fiche sans prix.
- La tendance de coût matière est celle du **batch** : deux formats d'une même fiche portent la même flèche, et c'est juste — c'est la même matière qui bouge.
- Aucune marge publiée tant qu'il manque un prix d'ingrédient (règle inchangée, appliquée par `margeEtCoef`).

## Preuves

- **Typecheck complet** `tsc -p tsconfig.check.json` : **5 erreurs**, exactement la baseline pré-existante (`supplier-splits` ×2, `valorisations/pdf` ×1, `valorisation/page` ×2). Aucune 6ᵉ.
- **`next build` exit 0**, 51+ pages.
- **Diff octet-pour-octet vide** sur les 4 fichiers entre la branche et le contenu validé localement.
- Typecheck **et** build rejoués depuis le contenu **extrait de la branche**, pas depuis le dossier de travail.
- Aucune migration : le modèle de données ne bouge pas (`recipe_formats` existe depuis le lot 46).

**Non vérifié à ce stade** : le rendu dans un navigateur sur getpilote.app — à faire après le merge.

author: prorochestvo
body:
Closes #6

## What the data showed

Analysed a read-only snapshot of the production database (2026-07-14 → 2026-08-04:
6140 runs at a 5-minute cadence, 24 735 checks). Full write-up in
[the issue comment](https://github.com/prorochestvo/yarddog/issues/6#issuecomment-5177454993).

- 29 runs were judged "internet down" → 11 reboots executed, 4 reboot attempts failed,
  14 skipped by cooldown.
- **In 28 of the 29 the raw uplink was provably alive**: both `ip` targets connected in
  19–1118 ms, and the ping collector recorded 4/4 ICMP replies from `8.8.8.8`, `1.1.1.1`
  and the ISP gateway in the same runs. Only the two HTTPS `domain` probes failed, both
  at exactly the 5 s `CHECK_TIMEOUT`.
- The 29th (2026-07-31 02:55) lost every target for a single sample and healed by the
  next run; its reboot attempt failed and was not what fixed it.
- Only one pair of consecutive down runs occurred in 21 days. Every other trigger was an
  isolated 5-minute sample between healthy runs.
- A further 17 runs had exactly one domain probe time out and correctly stayed "up". At a
  ~0.6 % per-probe failure rate, independent failures would coincide ~0.2 times in 21
  days; 29 were observed, so the two probes fail from a common cause — they share one DNS
  path, in production through the very router being rebooted.

## What changed

**Graded verdict** (`domain.Verdict`) — `down` (every `ip` target failed) is the only
state a reboot may follow. Every `domain` target failing while an `ip` target still
answers is `degraded`: recorded, announced, never rebooted. With no `ip` targets
configured the `domain` group remains the only evidence and still counts as `down`.

**In-run confirmation** — a `down` verdict is re-probed `CHECK_CONFIRMATIONS` times,
`CHECK_CONFIRM_DELAY` apart (persisted under a new `confirm` phase). One healthy sample
ends the run as `unconfirmed` and corrects the `internet_ok` written from the first
sample.

**Cross-run corroboration** — a reboot additionally requires the previous
`REBOOT_MIN_STREAK - 1` runs to have seen the outage, via a new
`RunRepository.RecentRuns`. A run that falls short ends as `unsustained`. Fail-closed: an
unreadable history withholds the reboot.

**Quieter Telegram** — neither guard sends a message; the run row and a log line carry the
record. `degraded` and cooldown-skip notices are edge-triggered, so the five identical
cooldown notices between 01:50 and 03:05 in the issue screenshot become one.

**Probe diagnostics** — a failed domain probe now carries the request stage it stalled in
(`stage=dns|connect|tls|request|response|body`) via `httptrace`, so "context deadline
exceeded" stops being the end of the investigation.

New optional config (defaults shown, all clamped): `CHECK_CONFIRMATIONS=2`,
`CHECK_CONFIRM_DELAY=20s`, `REBOOT_MIN_STREAK=2`. Setting confirmations to 0 and the
streak to 1 restores the previous behaviour exactly.

New `runs.outcome` values `degraded` / `unconfirmed` / `unsustained`, and exit code `6`
for "a failure was observed and deliberately not acted on".

Applied to the recorded history, these guards remove all 29 triggers, including the one
genuine blip that no reboot fixed.

## Also in this branch

- `test(httpapi)`: the overview-window subtest asserted a hardcoded `?since=` that
  `QueryService` floors at `now-31d`; it began failing on 2026-08-01 and blocked the test
  gate. Now derived from `time.Now()`.

## Verification

`go vet ./... && go test ./...` green (9/9 packages). New coverage: verdict grading table,
confirmation clearing and confirming a verdict, degraded never reaching the rebooter,
streak satisfied/unsatisfied/hard-run/query-error paths, edge-triggered notices, recovery
ending on a degraded verdict, `RecentRuns` against `:memory:`, config defaults and
clamping, and the probe stage tags.

## Operational follow-up (not in this PR)

The collector resolves DNS through the router itself (`systemd-resolved` → 192.168.1.1).
Pointing the host at upstream resolvers directly would remove the common-mode dependency
that produces these stalls at all. That is a change on the Pi, outside this repository.

In the Resources block's card layout, every resource kind renders a filled media band — a screenshot, a favicon on a kind-tinted wash, or a neutral wash — except a data app with no screenshot, which rendered a bare icon floating on the card's white body.
